extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor, literary critics, and philosophers interested in theories of the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic essay examining the causes, forms, and social function of the comic (what produces laughter and why). Extracts criteria for when something is laughable, illustrated with literary examples (Moliere, Don Quixote, Mark Twain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between particular/professional logic and universal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises from the clash between a specialised, customary way of reasoning valid within a particular circle and the general/common-sense logic of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: translating scientific ideas into 'feminine sensibility' (Moliere's Femmes savantes) produces comic effects. The page emphasises that professional logic can be valid within its circle yet untrue to the rest of the public; that contrast produces comedy. (No detailed scoring; treated as a stylistic source of incongruity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular kind of absurdity (inversion of common sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The absurdity present in the comic is not general absurdity but a definite inversion of common sense: moulding things to fit one's ideas instead of adapting ideas to things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Don Quixote seeing giants where others see windmills — 'seeking to mould things on an idea of one's own, instead of moulding one's ideas on things.' Bergson argues this particular inversion (not mere nonsense) is central to comic effect and recurs in many comic characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity, obstinacy, and automatism (following one idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic characters err through rigidity of mind or disposition—obstinacy, absentmindedness, automatism—so they stick to one path or idea irrespective of interruptions or contrary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common comic scenes reduce to a character 'FOLLOWING UP HIS ONE IDEA' and persistently recurring to it. This rigidity leads to seeing only what one wants and is a fundamental structural cause of comic absurdity (e.g., many Moliere scenes, Don Quixote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity as effect, not primary cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity in the comic is an effect that reflects the special nature of its cause (rigidity, inversion, social impertinence) rather than being the root cause itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson warns that merely inventing absurd situations per a general formula often fails; the comic's absurdity carries the 'particular essence' of its cause and thus must be of a definite kind. (Analytic caution rather than procedural rule.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-logic / relaxation of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic reasoning often mirrors dream reasoning: a relaxation of strict rules of logic, counterfeit reasoning lacking intellectual tension, where beginnings and ends of reasonings may be given without rigorous middle steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many witticisms are 'considerably abridged reasonings' that would deceive a 'mind dropping off to sleep.' This dream-like looseness produces relief from intellectual effort and can create humour. Examples and comparisons to dream mechanisms are given in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words and sound over meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: As relations between ideas become more superficial, comic effects shift toward play on words: the sound of words takes precedence over their meaning, producing nonsense or distorted meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson links this to dream-like dissociation of sense—speech becomes devoid of meaning and recombines into strange meanings (compared to scenes in Les Plaideurs). This is a specific mechanism for verbal humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / comic obsession
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrent images, phrases, or motifs that persistently reappear (with varying or implausible meanings) produce comic effect akin to dream obsessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: repeated burden of a song, images appearing in several successive dreams with different plausible meanings; on stage or in fiction such repetition can sound dream-like and comical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crescendo / progressive escalation toward absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: A gradual progression of concessions to absurdity—a first concession leads to a second, then to a more serious one—culminates in an intensified absurdity that produces comic sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson cites Moliere plays (e.g., Monsieur de Pourceaugnac, Bourgeois gentilhomme) where reasonable beginnings develop into sequences of absurdities, producing an increasing dream-like drift and eventual rousing of the audience when the extravagance peaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion/fusion of identities (self/not-self)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effects arise when a character or narration exhibits a strange fusion or confusion between persons (one being and yet another), producing statements or actions where the speaker alternately is and is not himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dream phenomena—feeling oneself both oneself and another—are paralleled in comic dialogues (Mark Twain's interview example) where the narrator asserts being one party yet speaks as an external storyteller, creating a specific comic absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playfulness and invitation to relaxation (audience sympathy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable often invites the audience to adopt, briefly, the comic character's relaxed/dream-like mental state; this mutual 'joining in the game' relieves the strain of continuous intellectual effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson notes an initial sympathy in the laugher who momentarily 'puts himself in his place' and enjoys the relief from tension; this sympathy is fleeting and part of why comic scenes can be pleasurable before correction is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as corrective / punitive social function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter functions as a social corrective: it is intended to humiliate or check impertinences that deviate from social norms; it punishes failings by making them objects of ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson emphasises that laughter 'avenges itself for the liberties taken with it' and is not necessarily benevolent or just; it operates spontaneously and collectively, striking at general results rather than individual fairness. This is a normative-social criterion for what becomes laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic types as models of impertinence; other varieties borrow comic quality by resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist predominant comic types (models of impertinence) and other varieties of the laughable derive their quality from resemblance to these types; the comic operates by resemblance to central forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson argues that isolating predominant types shows intervening varieties borrow their comic quality from resemblance to them. This provides a classificatory principle: to evaluate comic effects, consider their similarity to core comic types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity and fixed ideas are not inherently comic (contrast with laughable forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although certain comic logics resemble madness or fixed ideas, general insanity arouses pity rather than laughter; only a 'sane type of madness' compatible with overall mental health may be laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson warns against conflating clinical madness with comic absurdity—if the condition engenders pity or genuine suffering it ceases to be laughable. This is an anti-pattern: pathological illness is generally not a legitimate source of humour.
